### Contributing guidelines

- [X] I have read [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

### Module(s)

mini.clue

### Question

Suppose I’ve added `‘<Leader>’` as a trigger for mini.clue, and I want a sub-menu for `‘<Leader>x’`.

Up until now, I've been adding that menu by adding a `‘<Leader>x’` clue in my mini.clue config.

As far as I can tell, I can get the same effect by mapping `‘<Leader>x’` to `‘<Nop>’`.

Either way, when I type `‘<Leader>’` the x menu appears in the clue window.

Is that correct? Is there some additional benefit to adding a clue vs mapping the keys to `'<Nop>'`?

comment_data.body:
The main goal of 'mini.clue' is to show all available sequences of keys that actually *do* something, usually via available mappings.

To be more useful for nested mappings, after only small common part is typed 'mini.clue' also shows *something* to indicate that there are more keys under particular keys. For example, if there are `<Leader>ff` and `<Leader>fh` mappings, after pressing `<Leader>` there should be an entry for key `f` indicating that those two mappings are available. Those entries are generally refered to as ["group next key"](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e38547768b2e12bdd48b16b8cfdca2e3b7543e22/doc/mini-clue.txt#L227-L230).

There doesn't have to be anything extra done for it to be shown, especially no need to create a `<Nop>` mapping. But if you want to adjust the description of this group to be more helpful, adding a dedicated clue is [the recommended approach](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e38547768b2e12bdd48b16b8cfdca2e3b7543e22/doc/mini-clue.txt#L321-L325).

Does this make sense?

comment_data.body:
It makes sense. And it shows that I omitted an important part of my question: I know that the clue adds a description to the mapping group. I'm wondering whether there are any important differences between using a clue to add the description and using a `<Nop>` mapping to add the description.

As far as I can tell, once I’ve set up `<Leader>` as a trigger, the only reason to add a clue is to give a description to a mapping group, such as `<Leader>f`, like this:

```lua
clues = {
	{ mode = 'n', keys = '<Leader>f', desc = '+find'  },
}
```

I can get the same effect by creating a mapping to name the group. That is, mapping from `<Leader>f` to `<Nop>` and including a description in the mapping, like this:
```lua
vim.keymap.set('n', '<Leader>f', '<Nop>', { desc = '+find' } )
```

Adding the group descriptions via mappings has a nice benefit that I can name the groups in the same place where I define all of the mappings that have actions. Like this:

```lua
vim.keymap.set('n', '<Leader>f', '<Nop>', { desc = '+find' } )
vim.keymap.set('n', '<Leader>ff', '<Cmd>Pick files<CR>', { desc = 'find files' } )
```

If I use a clue to add the description, I define the mappings in one place, and the clues in another (the mini.clue config).

I can use either a clue or a `<Nop>` mapping to name the mapping group. As far as I can tell, the effect is the same either way.

What I don’t know: Are there important differences between the two mechanisms?

reply_data.body:
> What I don’t know: Are there important differences between the two mechanisms?

The 'mini.clue' was not initially designed to handle the case of "create a `<Nop>` mapping to set a group's name". If it works right now, then it is totally by coincidence. It also will probably keep working, unless some major and/or tricky rewrite will be done, which is not planned.

It *is* possible to add test for this case, but I think suggesting a dedicated clue is good enough here.
